cards.front: In adaptive immunity, what is multiplied before antigen arrives, and what is multiplied after?
cards.back: Variety (receptor shapes, from chance choice of gene segments) is multiplied before antigen. Numbers (cells of the clone that fits) are multiplied after it.
cards.quote: Variety is multiplied before antigen; numbers are multiplied after it.

cards.front: In the simple doubling model of a lymphocyte response, why does a second response to the same antigen arrive sooner?
cards.back: Memory leaves a larger starting clone, so fewer doublings are needed to reach enough cells.
cards.quote: Memory leaves a larger starting clone, so the next response needs fewer doublings and arrives sooner.

cards.front: In clonal selection, an antigen picks the few lymphocytes whose receptors fit, and they divide into a {{c1::clone}}, cells descended from one cell.
cards.back: Receptors are made first; antigen only selects.
cards.quote: receptors first, then antigen picks the few lymphocytes (B cells and T cells) that fit
cards.section: Receptors first: clonal selection

cards.front: How do the receptors of innate immunity differ from those of adaptive immunity?
cards.back: Innate receptors are encoded unchanged in the genome and recognize broad classes of microbes. Adaptive receptors are specific for particular antigens, and the response leaves memory.
cards.quote: Unlike innate immunity, whose receptors are encoded unchanged in the genome and recognize broad classes of microbes
cards.section: Receptors first: clonal selection

cards.front: How can a repertoire of millions of lymphocyte receptors cover microbes it never anticipated?
cards.back: One shape does not mean one target: a receptor ignores almost every molecule but can bind many that share the few features it contacts.
cards.why: One human CD8 T cell clone was estimated to respond to over a million different peptides.
cards.quote: That overlap is how a repertoire of millions covers microbes it never anticipated.
cards.section: Receptors first: clonal selection

cards.front: Describe the chain structure of an antibody and where it binds antigen.
cards.back: A Y-shaped protein of two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains. The tip of each arm, part heavy and part light chain, is the variable region that binds antigen.
cards.quote: An antibody is a Y-shaped protein of two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains
cards.section: Making the variety: segments, joins and pairs

cards.front: RAG enzymes cut beside chosen gene segments and the developing lymphocyte joins them, a process called {{c1::somatic recombination}}.
cards.back: It happens in body cells, not eggs or sperm, so it is not inherited.
cards.quote: RAG enzymes cut beside the chosen segments and the cell joins them: somatic recombination
cards.section: Making the variety: segments, joins and pairs

cards.front: Which gene segments are joined to make an antibody heavy chain, and which to make a light chain?
cards.back: Heavy chain: V (variable), D (diversity) and J (joining). Light chain: only V and J.
cards.quote: The letters stand for variable, diversity and joining
cards.section: Making the variety: segments, joins and pairs

cards.front: Which segments build the two chains of a conventional T cell receptor?
cards.back: The alpha chain joins V and J; the beta chain joins V, D and J.
cards.quote: a T cell pairs an alpha chain (V and J) with a beta chain (V, D and J)
cards.section: Making the variety: segments, joins and pairs

cards.front: What is junctional variation, and why do two lymphocytes that chose the same V, D and J segments usually still differ?
cards.back: Nucleotides are added or removed at each joint between segments, so the joined sequences differ even when the segments are the same.
cards.quote: nucleotides added or removed at each joint (junctional variation), so cells that chose the same segments usually still differ
cards.section: Making the variety: segments, joins and pairs

cards.front: Illustrative human counts: 5,520 heavy-chain V-D-J combinations; kappa light chain 40 V x 5 J; lambda light chain 30 V x 4 J. Assuming every combination works, how many heavy-light combinations are possible?
cards.why: A light chain is kappa or lambda (add); a B cell has a heavy and a light chain (multiply).
cards.quote: Pairing multiplies, because a B cell has a heavy chain and a light chain
cards.section: Making the variety: segments, joins and pairs

cards.front: When counting antibody light-chain combinations, why are the kappa and lambda counts added rather than multiplied?
cards.back: A given light chain is kappa or lambda, not both. Add for "or", multiply for "and".
cards.quote: Add: 200 + 120 = 320, because a light chain is kappa or lambda.
cards.section: Making the variety: segments, joins and pairs

cards.front: Suppose B cells could use only kappa light chains (40 V x 5 J) with 5,520 heavy-chain combinations. How many heavy-light combinations are possible, assuming all work?
cards.quote: Kappa: 40 V x 5 J = 200.
cards.section: Making the variety: segments, joins and pairs

cards.front: A hypothetical person has 8 lambda J segments instead of 4 (30 V), with kappa 40 V x 5 J and 5,520 heavy-chain combinations. How many heavy-light combinations, assuming all work?
cards.why: Same rule: heavy combinations x (kappa + lambda combinations).
cards.quote: receptor combinations = (V x D x J for heavy) x [(V x J for kappa) + (V x J for lambda)]
cards.section: Making the variety: segments, joins and pairs

cards.front: The combinatorial count of about 1.8 million heavy-light pairs is a simplified model. Name one way it overstates and one way it understates real receptor diversity.
cards.back: Overstates: it assumes every combination works and is equally used, which real repertoires do not. Understates: junctional variation multiplies the sequences many times over.
cards.quote: The receptor count assumes every combination works and is equally used; real repertoires do not.
cards.section: Going deeper: what the simple models leave out

cards.front: Which receptor change happens only after antigen, and only in B cells? What does it do?
cards.back: Somatic hypermutation: point mutations in the variable region, with better binders favoured, so antibody affinity rises. Conventional T cell receptors do not undergo it.
cards.quote: B cells only: somatic hypermutation, point mutations in the variable region, with better binders favoured, so antibody affinity (how tightly it binds) rises
cards.section: Making the variety: segments, joins and pairs

cards.front: A mutation abolishes RAG enzyme activity in developing lymphocytes. Predict the effect on antibodies and T cell receptors.
cards.back: Neither can be assembled, so the variable receptors of jawed-vertebrate antibodies and T cell receptors are lost. RAG enzymes cut beside the gene segments that somatic recombination joins.
cards.quote: Each tip is encoded by gene segments, short stretches of DNA
cards.section: Making the variety: segments, joins and pairs

cards.front: Newly hatched chickens had either the bursa or the thymus removed, then were tested for antibody production and skin-graft rejection. What result showed two lymphocyte lineages?
cards.back: Without the bursa, antibody was largely lost but grafts were still rejected, more slowly; without the thymus, graft rejection was impaired. Bursa-derived B cells and thymus-derived T cells.
cards.why: One lineage would predict both jobs crippled by either loss.
cards.quote: The birds showed the second pattern: without the bursa, antibody was largely lost while grafts were still rejected, only more slowly
cards.section: Where B and T cells come from: a chicken's bursa

cards.front: In the chicken bursa and thymus removal experiments, why were the birds irradiated after surgery?
cards.back: To deplete lymphocytes that had already left the organ, so the removal's effect was not masked.
cards.quote: then irradiated them to deplete lymphocytes that had already left the organ
cards.section: Where B and T cells come from: a chicken's bursa

cards.front: Mammals have no bursa. Where do B cells and T cells develop in humans and mice?
cards.back: B cells: from blood-forming stem cells in the fetal liver, then the bone marrow. T cells: mature in the thymus.
cards.quote: in humans and mice B cells develop from blood-forming stem cells in the fetal liver and then the bone marrow
cards.section: Where B and T cells come from: a chicken's bursa

cards.front: How does antigen recognition by a B cell receptor differ from that of a conventional (alpha-beta) T cell receptor?
cards.back: A B cell receptor binds intact antigen in lymph or blood, without processing. A T cell receptor binds no free antigen; it reads a short peptide on an MHC molecule on another cell.
cards.quote: a B cell's receptor binds intact antigen in lymph or blood, without processing
cards.section: Antibodies and killer T cells: class I and class II

cards.front: Some descendants of an activated B cell become {{c1::plasma cells}}, which secrete large amounts of antibody.
cards.quote: some descendants become plasma cells, B cells that secrete large amounts of antibody
cards.section: Antibodies and killer T cells: class I and class II

cards.front: Most antibodies do not kill microbes on their own. Name three ways they act instead.
cards.back: Neutralize (coat a virus or toxin so it cannot attach to cells), opsonize (tag a microbe for phagocytes to engulf), and activate complement.
cards.quote: Most antibodies do not kill microbes on their own.
cards.section: Antibodies and killer T cells: class I and class II

cards.front: Cytotoxic T cells from virus-infected mice were tested against infected cells from mice of the same or a different MHC type. What happened, and what does it show?
cards.back: They killed infected cells only when the cells shared their MHC type. A T cell recognizes antigen only together with MHC.
cards.quote: They killed infected cells only when the cells shared their MHC type.
cards.section: Antibodies and killer T cells: class I and class II

cards.front: MHC class I: which cells carry it, what peptides does it display, and which T cells read it?
cards.back: Almost all nucleated cells; peptides from proteins made inside the cell; CD8 cytotoxic T cells, which kill the cell by triggering apoptosis.
cards.quote: MHC class I is on almost all nucleated cells.
cards.section: Antibodies and killer T cells: class I and class II

cards.front: MHC class II: which cells normally carry it, what peptides does it display, and which T cells read it?
cards.back: Antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B cells); peptides from material the cell has taken in; CD4 helper T cells.
cards.why: Memory aid: CD8 x class I = 8, CD4 x class II = 8.
cards.quote: MHC class II is normally found on antigen-presenting cells: dendritic cells, macrophages and B cells.
cards.section: Antibodies and killer T cells: class I and class II

cards.front: What do CD4 helper T cells do after reading peptide on MHC class II?
cards.back: They release cytokines (signaling proteins) that activate macrophages and help B cells.
cards.quote: CD4 helper T cells read class II and release signaling proteins (cytokines; see JAK-STAT signaling) that activate macrophages and help B cells.
cards.section: Antibodies and killer T cells: class I and class II

cards.front: A virus blocks the display of peptides on MHC class I in the liver cells it infects. Predict the effect on killing by CD8 T cells, and why.
cards.back: Infected cells escape CD8 killing. CD8 cytotoxic T cells recognize viral peptides only when they are displayed on class I.
cards.quote: It displays peptides from proteins made inside the cell, so a virus-infected liver cell shows viral peptides.
cards.section: Antibodies and killer T cells: class I and class II

cards.front: Atlantic cod have lost MHC class II and CD4. Which antigen-presentation route is missing in cod, and which remains?
cards.back: Missing: display of peptides from engulfed material on class II to CD4 helper T cells. The lesson names no other loss, so class I display to CD8 T cells is presumably intact.
cards.why: Rests on the pairing CD4 with class II and CD8 with class I.
cards.quote: Atlantic cod, for example, have lost MHC class II and CD4.
cards.section: Adaptive immunity compared: lampreys and jawed vertebrates

cards.front: After a primary response, why can plasma antibody fall while memory remains?
cards.back: Antibody comes mainly from plasma cells and turns over. Memory B and T cells are a separate store that secretes no antibody while it waits, then drives the faster secondary response.
cards.quote: Memory B and T cells are a separate store that secretes no antibody while it waits, then drives the faster secondary response.
cards.section: Memory, vaccines, mothers' antibodies and blood groups

cards.front: Contrast active and passive immunity.
cards.back: Active: made by your own lymphocytes after infection or a vaccine; leaves memory. Passive: antibody made in another body; works at once, lasts until broken down, leaves no memory.
cards.quote: only active immunity, from infection or a vaccine (antigen without the disease), leaves this store; passive immunity does not
cards.section: Memory, vaccines, mothers' antibodies and blood groups

cards.front: A newborn foal gets no colostrum in its first days. Predict its maternal antibody level, and why.
cards.back: Low. In horses the placenta lets little antibody through, so the newborn gets maternal antibody mainly from colostrum absorbed by its gut in the first day or so.
cards.quote: the newborn gets antibody mainly from colostrum, the first milk, absorbed by its gut in the first day or so
cards.section: Memory, vaccines, mothers' antibodies and blood groups

cards.front: In humans the antibody class {{c1::IgG}} crosses the placenta before birth.
cards.back: A form of passive immunity.
cards.quote: In humans the antibody class IgG crosses the placenta before birth.
cards.section: Memory, vaccines, mothers' antibodies and blood groups

cards.front: In the ABO system, group O red cells carry the unmodified {{c1::H}} antigen, not no antigen.
cards.quote: group O cells carry the unmodified H antigen, not no antigen
cards.section: Memory, vaccines, mothers' antibodies and blood groups

cards.front: A group AB person receives group O red cells. Do the recipient's ABO antibodies attack them? Why?
cards.back: No. Group AB serum has neither anti-A nor anti-B, and O cells carry H antigen, not A or B.
cards.quote: group O serum contains anti-A and anti-B, and group AB serum neither
cards.section: Memory, vaccines, mothers' antibodies and blood groups

cards.front: How can group O serum contain anti-A and anti-B before any transfusion, given clonal selection?
cards.back: These antibodies are thought to arise in early life in response to similar sugars on gut bacteria and food.
cards.quote: These antibodies are thought to arise in early life in response to similar sugars on gut bacteria and food
cards.section: Memory, vaccines, mothers' antibodies and blood groups

cards.front: An Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive fetus and is exposed to its red cells. Predict the risk to a later Rh-positive fetus, and why.
cards.back: Its red cells can be destroyed. She makes anti-Rh only after exposure, and that antibody is mostly IgG, which crosses the placenta in a later pregnancy.
cards.quote: An Rh-negative mother exposed to an Rh-positive fetus's red cells can make anti-Rh IgG that crosses the placenta in a later pregnancy
cards.section: Memory, vaccines, mothers' antibodies and blood groups

cards.front: Why can a first mismatched ABO transfusion cause an immediate reaction, while a first exposure to Rh-positive cells in an Rh-negative person does not?
cards.back: ABO antibodies are already present before any transfusion and bind at once. Anti-Rh is normally made only after exposure, so a first exposure meets a primary response.
cards.quote: an Rh-negative person normally makes anti-Rh only after exposure, and most such antibodies are IgG
cards.section: Memory, vaccines, mothers' antibodies and blood groups

cards.front: What is the mechanism of an immediate, IgE-mediated allergic reaction?
cards.back: IgE against a harmless antigen sits on mast cells; allergen binds and cross-links it, and the mast cells release histamine and other mediators within minutes.
cards.quote: IgE sits on mast cells, and when allergen binds and cross-links it the mast cells release histamine and other mediators within minutes
cards.section: Memory, vaccines, mothers' antibodies and blood groups

cards.front: Self-reactive clones are normally deleted or silenced during development, and regulatory T cells restrain others; autoimmunity is a failure of this {{c1::tolerance}}.
cards.quote: Normally self-reactive clones are deleted or silenced during development, and regulatory T cells restrain others; autoimmunity is a failure of this tolerance.
cards.section: Memory, vaccines, mothers' antibodies and blood groups

cards.front: What receptors do lamprey lymphocyte-like cells use instead of antibodies, and what are they built from?
cards.back: Variable lymphocyte receptors, assembled in each cell from a library of leucine-rich-repeat modules.
cards.quote: sea lamprey (Petromyzon marinus) lymphocyte-like cells carry variable lymphocyte receptors, assembled in each cell from a library of leucine-rich-repeat modules
cards.section: Adaptive immunity compared: lampreys and jawed vertebrates

cards.front: Lampreys and jawed vertebrates both have adaptive immunity. Which parts are probably shared ancestry, and which are convergence?
cards.back: The lymphocyte lineages are probably inherited from a common vertebrate ancestor; the variable receptors evolved separately. Both follow clonal selection: variety first, antigen choosing, the fitting clone expanding.
cards.quote: the variable receptors evolved separately in jawless and jawed vertebrates
cards.section: Adaptive immunity compared: lampreys and jawed vertebrates

cards.front: Do insects have lymphocytes?
cards.back: No. Invertebrates such as insects rely on innate defenses, though some innate systems can be primed.
cards.quote: Invertebrates, such as insects, have no lymphocytes and rely on innate defenses
cards.section: Adaptive immunity compared: lampreys and jawed vertebrates

cards.front: After SARS-CoV-2 infection, spike antibody drifted down while spike-specific memory B cells were more abundant at six months than at one month. Does falling antibody mean lost memory? How would you test it?
cards.back: No. Measure antibody, memory B cells and CD4 and CD8 T cells separately, sampling the same people repeatedly, and report each trend. None of these readouts measures protection.
cards.why: Antibody comes from plasma cells; memory cells are a separate store.
cards.quote: Memory B cells can persist or even rise while antibody falls, as they did here.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: An antibody half-life was estimated from different people sampled at different times. What sampling design gives a better estimate of each person's trend?
cards.back: Paired longitudinal samples: sample each person repeatedly rather than different people at different times.
cards.quote: Sample each person repeatedly (paired longitudinal samples), not different people at different times
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Antibody levels, memory B cell counts and T cell assays are all measured after infection. Why can none of them alone show that a person is protected?
cards.back: None is a measure of protection. Protection needs its own endpoint, such as reinfection rates.
cards.quote: State the limit plainly: none of these readouts is a measure of protection.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Spike antibody fell with an apparent half-life of about 140 days. If it kept declining at that rate, roughly what fraction would remain after 280 days?
cards.back: 280 / 140 = 2 half-lives; (1/2)^2 = 0.25, about one quarter.
cards.quote: with an apparent half-life of about 140 days in a cross-sectional fit
cards.section: Design problem
